utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. Could you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning. This is Case Number IT-97-24-T, the Prosecutor versus Milomir Stakic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: And the appearances, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Nicholas Koumjian with Ruth Karper for the Prosecution. Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Branko Lukic and Mr. John Ostojic for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Before we start with the cross-examination, I want to come back to an issue we discussed during the 65 ter (i) meeting. And I want to do it once again in the presence of Dr. Stakic. That is the question of signatures. And as I mentioned already before, the Trial Chamber is of the opinion that, in principle, it is necessary to have an expert witness on the question whether or not one can find out if or if not the signatures -- different signatures we have found until now on certain copies are written by Dr. Stakic or not. And it could not be necessary, as it was indicated by the Defence, if -- I couldn't call it an agreement, but if there would be a statement by Dr. Stakic. First of all, I have to emphasise once again that of course, the right of Dr. Stakic to remain silent and the right of the Defence to say nothing, quite clear. But I don't know whether or not you have discussed this issue with your client, and furthermore, the question: In case you would decide that you would say your client would advise you that, as regards the one or other signature, this could be accepted, this could be done in several different ways. Either by saying: "We are not contesting," or by saying "The one or the other signature, that's right, that's the signature of our client." Or it would be, as I said in the beginning of the trial, of course, the right of Dr. Stakic to make his own statement, if he so wants, in agreement with the Defence. Or it would be a possibility, and it was discussed by the Bench, that if it would be regarded as appropriate by the Defence, that Dr. Stakic could appear only, and only limited to this issue, and appear as a witness in the case. And we would take care that no other issue would be discussed in the framework of such statement. So therefore, had you had the possibility to discuss the issue with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. It was my task, if I can put it that way to meet and to try to discuss the signatures on some of the documents, although we did receive additional documents which purport to have Dr. Stakic's signature. And my plan was to meet with Dr. Stakic either Monday afternoon or Tuesday afternoon. But due to some personal commitments of my own, I was not able to go to the Detention Centre yesterday. Mr. Lukic did. I still maintained a copy of the documents and personally was going to check with Dr. Stakic on that. Just so the Chamber knows, we will go through that and have a complete report by next Wednesday with respect to the documents that we either contest, or the documents we will not contest with respect to signatures. There is, just briefly checking with him, some discrepancy on the signatures; however, -- or at least that's our position, again. We have to take a closer look at it. The stamp is on some of the signatures. I have just been passing in between the breaks and we check with Dr. Stakic on that. So we would reserve the right to do that and to report back to the Chamber by next Wednesday. I know we're meeting on Tuesday, but because of the four-day break, we might need to have Monday and Tuesday afternoon to meet with him on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The time is running, and as we mentioned before, it is necessary to start with -- if necessary -- such an expert witness as soon as possible because such expertise normally takes two or more months. And therefore, it has to be decided immediately. But seeing, and respecting, your readiness to discuss this issue seriously with your client, I think it's appropriate that we can proceed as suggested, if the OTP doesn't object, and then we could discuss in toto all the signatures on the -- yeah. On all the documents we have in list 1, 2, and 3, and the one we got two pieces of paper -- it would be very neutral -- we got from the Witness Murselovic. And if we can go through all these documents next Wednesday, I think it should be appropriate.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would just suggest that I get together with the Defence after they have had a chance to discuss it with their client. We do not necessarily maintain that every signature that is above a line with the accused's name, is the accused. I've seen some where the word "Za" meaning for, appears before the signature. So we may not be in dispute that some of these were signed by somebody else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may, Your Honour, on this point --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Can we conclude that it's then the real and the final deadline next Wednesday on this issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have one other item if I may, Your Honour, related to this. Would it be appropriate if the Defence, during the cross-examination, submit to this witness signatures of parties including Dr. Stakic in order to have him verify or select which signature he deems to be the one that is Dr. Stakic's? Without going into much detail, we would propose that there's at least five to ten such signatures on a signature card similar to the photo identification card that the OTP proposed earlier, during the beginning of the trial. We would just like leave of Court to do that. We don't want to surprise the Chamber, nor the witness and try to submit this signature block, if you will, to a witness. We have a differing view on some of the testimony, without going into it in detail. So that would be one way in which we think we can establish what this Chamber and this Tribunal is trying to achieve, and that is truth, to see the veracity of each of the witnesses and, at the end of the day, to determine the truth as to what occurred on or about the area of Prijedor in 1992. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. Observations by the OTP to this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, we are opposed to having experiments conducted in the courtroom. I leave it to Your Honours' discretion, but we would be opposed to that being done in the courtroom. I would like to bring up another matter just related to this witness. We need -- for his schedule it's not possible for him to stay beyond Thursday. I just hope we can complete his cross-examination and all questioning by Thursday. If not, we're going to have to work out another date to bring him back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Right. I think we all share the view that this can be and must be concluded until Thursday. But I don't know how you want to proceed. We have numerous signatures, and if you, of course, have them in a comparative approach, I can't identify any obstacles. And so therefore, let's wait and see what will happen in general. There shouldn't be any objections from our side.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. And I do have one last point distantly related to this witness, if we're considering some administrative issues if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Last Friday, Mr. Inayat testified, in part, both during the direct examination on behalf of the OTP and some of the questions from the Defence late last Friday, we are requesting based on Mr. Inayat's -- and I apologise to him if I'm mispronouncing his name, based on his testimony that it may take anywhere from one to three days to provide us with an index from their either Zylab [sic] programme or from whichever computer software programme they are utilising, in order to determine what, if any, additional documents we have not received which we may deem, and I understand the rule and that it's the Prosecutor decides if it's relevant, pursuant to Rule 68. And without going into too much detail, if the Court examines the threshold issues that we examined, one being namely propaganda, what we would like to determine and we think it's important although it's up to the Court to decide is whether or not the propaganda on all three sides would be considered relevant in Prijedor municipality, and whether or not the response by some, whether on the Serbian side or the Bosniak/Muslim side, or the Croatian side were responsive or replying to propaganda initiated by one of the three sides. We received from Kozarski Vjesnik the propaganda, in part, of the Serbs. We think it would be relevant to receive that propaganda, if any, from the other two sides. We think the index will help establish that. We believe that under the broad interpretation of Rule 68, that that would be deemed exculpatory, in part. Secondly, we have been receiving from the OTP, generously, additional Rule 68 materials. For example, I believe yesterday we received, dated May 28th, additional documents with Tab Number 881. And we appreciate that, so we want to thank them in open court for that. But we believe there are yet additional documents, if we were provided this index which, under the time constraints that I understand the OTP is under and the specific unit that Mr. Inayat's team one is a team leader of, if we would have that, we would be able to discern and determine which additional documents we may need. And at that point, either an ex parte evaluation can be done by the Chamber, or the OTP can determine whether it even wants to proceed on that step, or merely provide us a copy of the documents that we're requesting. Because as we suggested last Friday, I'm not sure if it was eloquent or clear enough, we do not have access to documents which have been the original, which have been removed and are no longer in the Prijedor municipality, namely the four to six institutions that the OTP and the team leaders removed those documents from. So it's necessary for our defence to be able to see, in totality, these documents to make a determination as to whether or not it would fit within our defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would have a great deal to say regarding this request. My request is can we deal with this after the witness is finished, because it can take a long time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I understand. I only want to invite the parties to come to an agreement between the parties before the Bench has to decide on this. But the parties should know, and I believe they have already got the impression, that the Bench is not too enthusiastic on propaganda and its probative value in this case when it came to the admission of evidence in the beginning on the basis of the testimony of Dr. Donia. But please, try to come to a solution among the parties, and let's now start with the witness today. May the witness be brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Good morning. Please be seated. And you are prepared for cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We may start immediately. And thank you for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Cross-examined by Mr. Lukic:

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Dr. Mujadzic. My name is Branko Lukic, and together with Mr. John Ostojic, we represent the defence of Dr. Stakic before this Tribunal. I should like to ask for your assistance in clarifying certain issues which are of interest to the Defence, just as you have assisted the Prosecution in their case. In light of the fact that we speak the same language, we're likely to pose problems to interpreters. I know that it's not natural to make pauses between questions and answer, but please bear in mind that after I have finished asking my question, to wait a little, perhaps have a look at the screen to see whether the interpretation has come out, and then proceed with your answer. Thank you. Let me begin with page 8, line 17 of the transcript of yesterday's testimony.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but I do not see anything on my screen. Could the screen be switched on, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I will indicate the pages and the lines from the transcript, but I will, at the same time, quote your words. I am indicating the page numbers and the line numbers only for the purposes of the record. So please, do not be confused with that. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. You told us about the steering committee of the SDA in Prijedor on page 8, line 17 of Monday's transcript. You said that "at that time in the Prijedor SDA, there were two factions within this board. Each of them supported their own candidate." Can you explain to us the differences between these two factions at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The substantial differences concerned the overall organisation of the Prijedor municipality. The Prijedor municipality consisted, and still does, of Kozarac, Omarska, Ljubija, Prijedor town, and the area which is called Brdo. Out of these segments, so to speak, of the municipality, the town of Kozarac had its characteristic identity, because it is a much older town than the town of Prijedor. Its origins date back to the 13th century. Likewise, Ljubija was also distinct in this sense as part of the municipality because of the mine ore complex. And then there was the town of Prijedor, which can also be considered as a separate entity within this municipality. So the factions that you refer to were, first of all, regional in their character because certain areas supported their own candidate, and other areas had their own. So these differences were regional, so to speak, in their nature. As it is usually the case with the elections, every area has their own candidate to support.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for your answer. On page 11, line 24, still Monday's transcript, you testify about a census. Is it correct that the results of this census were never verified?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not directly involved in the census of the population because there were municipal boards at the level of the municipality that were in charge of the census. These boards were established pursuant to a proposal issued by various parties, members of the parliament in the municipality. This proposal was accepted by the assembly and was forwarded to the republic commission, the republic board for census. And pursuant to that proposal, this commission was established and its members appointed, thereby guaranteeing the regularity and legality of the census. There were several such commissions and several persons in charge of taking the census. This commission was a multiethnic commission and multiparty in its character as well. So the results of the census were first reviewed by the commission, and then after that, the results were forwarded to the commission which functioned at the level of the republic. And from there, I believe that they were forwarded to the republic institute for statistics where once again the results were reviewed and verified. I must admit that personally, I don't know that there have been any objections as to the census of the population in Prijedor, so I don't know whether there was any need to verify anything subsequently. I don't remember anyone raising the issue of authenticity of the population census in Prijedor or the credibility of this census.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You're not familiar with the objections that the SDS had as to the results of the census?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that they objected to the results of the elections, and they did so on several occasions.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you not aware of the fact that they criticised the results of the census as well?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we therefore conclude that you're not -- you don't know whether the results of the census were ever verified?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the Prijedor municipality or the results of the census in the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I'm referring to the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina as a whole.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already said that I do not remember having heard any objections or criticism as to the results of the population census, so I'm afraid I'm unable to answer your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: That is also a legitimate answer. Whenever you feel you're not able to provide us with an answer, please feel free to say so. On page 15, line 11, we're still on Monday's transcript, at the very end of the page and then throughout the following page, page 16, you explained to us how Mr. Milosevic wanted to revoke the right of the republics in terms of voting, by trying to introduce a one-person, one-vote principle. Do you know whether the autonomous provinces, Kosovo and Vojvodina which were two component parts of Serbia had the same right of vote at the level of the federation as the republics?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that your question? I think that you are only partially right. As far as I am familiar with the constitution of the former federative Republic of Yugoslavia, this equality was equally reflected in the Presidency of Yugoslavia after Tito's death which had eight members, eight members of the presidency. Each republic had their representative to the presidency, as was the case with the autonomous provinces. As for the two Chambers of the parliament of the federation of Yugoslavia, it consisted of the chamber of republics and provinces, the members of which were elected as follows: There were 12 members, 12 representatives, from each of the republics, and eight members, as far as I can recall, from the two provinces. So they had fewer representatives in this segment of the parliament than the republics. So the influence of the provinces was significantly reduced when compared to the influence of the republics. As for the first part of your question, that is, the abolishment of the right to equal vote, I don't know whether this was merely your allegation or if you wish me to respond to your question.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I believe you have provided us with a sufficient response. Thank you. Can we, therefore, agree that at the level of the head of state, which was a collective body which was introduced after Tito's death, of course, I'm referring to the presidency of Yugoslavia, that Serbia together with Montenegro and two of its provinces had four votes and that it could not be outvoted in any way?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you implying the assumption that at any rate, Montenegro was giving its vote, according to your hypothesis, to some sort of Serb majority within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was that a customary occurrence at the time? Did Montenegro ever vote against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right about that. That was the case at the time. Serbia and Montenegro always voted together. If you remember, if you're familiar with those days, you will also recall the so-called Jogurt revolution through which Milosevic was able to impose his men, to install Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. his people in both provinces and also in Montenegro. So you're quite right about that. He always had four votes within the federal presidency in Yugoslavia, and there was no way he could be outvoted.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why was it then necessary to introduce the one-person/one-vote principle?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The principle of one-person/one-vote was not the result of any realistic threat posed to the Milosevic regime or any realistic threat posed to the Serbian population in Yugoslavia in general. The introduction of this principle was the result of Milosevic's wish to dominate Yugoslavia and to have the majority on his side. He did not -- he was not satisfied with the balance with this ratio of forces within the presidency. He wanted to have the majority of votes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As for the one-person/one-vote principle, although I -- although it is accepted in all western countries and in the majority of democratic systems in the world, do you still believe that the principle in question was inadequate and that it could not be applied to Yugoslavia as a whole; and if so, would you give us your reasons why?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection, relevance as to the relevance of this witness's views of what the politics of Yugoslavia should have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Actually, I'd be happy to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I know --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: -- Please understand, we have not to decide on politics, on political questions, what would have been the right political solution and so on. I know we can't have a clear distinction and a clear line, but I would really ask you to concentrate on both with your questions and your answers, to concentrate on the relevant matters of this case where we have to come at the end of the day to the conclusion whether or not there is a criminal responsibility of a concrete person or not. But I don't -- I know very well, it's different to find the correct line. But please bear this in mind, both with the questions and the length of your answer. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Should I move on, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: We could first of all hear the short answer of the witness, and then you may proceed. Do you remember the question? Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do, Your Honour. I'll do my best and try to be as brief as possible. You're right. This principle is followed by most of the countries in Europe. However, most of the European countries are one nation countries, such as France and Germany. On the other hand, Yugoslavia was a federation which was made up of several different republics, which in distant past were independent countries with a very long tradition. So this was the reason why Yugoslavia was specific in this regard. And this was the reason why Yugoslavia required a different kind of voting and not the one-person/one-vote principle.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So this principle was primarily applied to protect the peoples that lived within Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that also mean that this one-person/one-vote principle could be applied in Bosnia-Herzegovina as Yugoslavia on a small scale?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the context that you speak about, Bosnia-Herzegovina could not be compared to Yugoslavia. Yugoslavia was composed of geographically homogenous wholes and it was a state which came into existence by an agreement following World War I. Bosnia-Herzegovina, on the other hand, is a state that was created as far back as the 10th century. It's past is a thousand years long. Its past has been in existence as an entity for a thousand years. So perhaps there is a degree of similarity in as far as Bosnia-Herzegovina, indeed, is a state composed of three peoples with equal rights. But unlike in Yugoslavia, in Bosnia-Herzegovina, there weren't any different geographical entities. As I said yesterday, in Western Bosnia, there were only Serbs. There was a part of Bosnia where there were only Croats. It wasn't like that. The whole of Bosnia-Herzegovina was mixed. Even small villages were. So these are two very different things and there can be no comparison in that context between Yugoslavia and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the concept, the constitutiveness of a people, constitutionality of a people?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with that concept.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was it valid before the war in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Bosnia and Herzegovina had its three constitutional peoples.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Nowadays, after the principle was abolished during the war, is it in force in Bosnia-Herzegovina today?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we're talking about the Dayton agreements, but I will try to provide an answer to this question. By the Dayton agreements, which did not entirely reflect the will of the people of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosnia and Herzegovina was established as a state consisting of two entities. One was Republika Srpska, and the other was the federation. One of the entities, Republika Srpska, did really bear in its name the title "Republika Srpska" which would lead one to believe that it was an entity that belonged only to Serbs, and the other entity, the federation, was allegedly a community of Bosniaks and Croats. And that's how the first constitution was drafted in both of these entities. However, the Dayton accords were merely a peace agreement, and as such, it does not imply constitutional provisions for a given country so that later on, an initiative was started, and it's nearing implementation in the federation. It's almost implemented, that all three peoples should be constitutional peoples in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina, which means that both in the federation that, at first, only implied Bosniaks and Croats. Serbs now should, too, be a constitutional people. And by the same reciprocity, also in the territory of Republika Srpska, Bosniaks and Croats should become constitutional groups. This is not the case now, but such reciprocal solutions should soon begin to take place. The high representative of UNHCR for Bosnia-Herzegovina also confirmed this. I'm sorry this explanation proved a bit lengthy, but it was a complex question, so I did find that I had to provide a lengthy explanation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know how many Bosniak delegates there are currently in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. assembly of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: I'm not prepared to admit questions being not of relevance for the case. The time before and the incidents leading to the period of time which is the subject matter of our case is, of course, of importance, but not the time after.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Thank you, Your Honour. I'll move on.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. We shall leave this area now. And I will ask you something related to your statement on Monday's transcript, page 15, page 16 where you speak about the whole of Yugoslavia breaking up into the pro-Milosevic and pro-Yugoslavia camps and those who were against it. You also say that this affected Prijedor. Do you believe that this division was also the main course for the war that broke out in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic, please excuse me, but the question appears illogical to me. Whether someone supported Milosevic or not, can this lead to a war?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The implication is that the war was a consequence of a division, a conflict, so that was my question.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The true causes of this war lie much deeper. If you ask me what the causes were, I could try to provide an answer; however, your question implies that it was this division that caused the war in the first place, which I do not agree with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You mentioned the pro-Yugoslavia parties, at that time, the SDS, the Serbian Reconstruction Movement, and the Radical Party. Against this were the HDZ, the SDA, the Social Democrats, and part of the Communist Party. Is this correct? Can you recall this?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you can please remember I said that the SDA, in its programme, had, as one of its most prominent features, the preservation of Yugoslavia. The SDA was one of the most interested parties of Bosniaks, as such, were people with the greatest interest in preserving Yugoslavia as a community of six different peoples all with equal rights, because Yugoslavia, as such, guaranteed security and stability to the Bosniak people. But speaking of two different concepts of Yugoslavia, the SDA did not advocate Milosevic's view of Yugoslavia, Milosevic's idea of Yugoslavia, but it did support Yugoslavia. So this division is not really reliable.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I was only quoting you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: I would object because that misquoted the witness. The witness in that answer indicated that these were parties with a certain national zeal. He never identified those parties as being the pro-Yugoslav parties. It's on -- for some reason, my page and line numbers are slightly different than Mr. Lukic's. But on my page 16, it would be line 16, if we're talking about parties based on a certain national zeal such as the Party of Democratic Action, the Croatian -- I withdraw. I don't want to go into it any further. I think I slightly misread it before I intervened. Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: It would be indeed for all our assistance, also the Bench couldn't follow the quotations. I don't know why, what's wrong today. Apparently we have different numbers of pages as regard the 28th of May, it's only slightly different. But unfortunately, as regards the 27th, it is already the -- it's starting page 3568. I don't know. On the basis of Livenote, we have to take care using that, it's a different numbering. I don't know why today. But please, we rely on you quoting careful the entire sentence, and there will be no problem at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I'll certainly do my best, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you, in your statement, contend that the SDA would place a condition on staying in Yugoslavia if Croatia stayed and in order to achieve the principle of equidistance?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that Yugoslavia was by definition a community of six states with equal rights, including Slovenia, Croatia, Serbia, Montenegro, Macedonia, and the two provinces. Any of these states or republics -- should any of these states or republics secede, which was almost certain as far as Slovenia was concerned at that moment, the balance you mentioned was destroyed, especially in the presidents where the ratio was four against four, and now already the ratio would be four against three in Milosevic's favour. So that already would destroy the balance and destroy the possibility of having equal rights for all the republics. Bosnia said that it wanted to preserve Yugoslavia at all costs, even if only Croatia stayed because Croatia was not that far down the road of secession at that time as Slovenia was.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can you then, please, tell us whether the SDA, after Croatia's secession, had a definite plan for the secession of Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you would please just think back to that period, and I would like to briefly present Your Honours with the situation in that period, the situation which the then presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina was facing. What you are saying about the SDA, the question is no, there was no definite plan of secession. There were different initiatives, various options so that if you remember, there was the so-called Belgrade initiative led by Professor Muhamed Pilipovic [as interpreted] and a political group surrounding him. They went to Belgrade to negotiate with Milosevic in order to try to secure for Bosnia-Herzegovina in possible rump Yugoslavia a certain status through new constitutional solutions. This initiative, unfortunately, failed. It fell through. It was obvious that Milosevic offered no such solutions as to guarantee the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina equal rights in rump Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We are talking about Mr. Muhamed Filipovic. Which party did he belong to?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: For a certain period of time, he belonged to the Party of Democratic Action and then, after that, Muslim/Bosniak organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When he went to these negotiations, which party was it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Muslim/Bosniak organisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I asked you about the SDA's plans.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, all parties, with the exception of the SDS, at the level of presidency considered jointly options for the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore, Mr. Filipovic's initiative, and the initiative of Mr. Zulfikar Pasic had political backing from all parties which amounts to the same thing as if all parties were taking part in this attempt to reach an agreement. It was only later, in February, so, much later after the secession of Croatia, after the SDS walked out of the parliament and proclaimed its Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. own Serbian republic, and a long time after the Autonomous Region of Krajina was proclaimed, with a view to secession and annexation by Serbia, it was quite clear that at that point, the issue became so complex that people had to decide about it on a referendum. So the parliament voted a referendum. And the question should be put to the people whether they were in favour of a sovereign Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would just like to go back to Professor Muhamed Filipovic for a moment and ask you, are you familiar with the fact that he did, indeed, accept the Belgrade initiative, but that the initiative was rejected by the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge he brought this initiative before a party meeting, and after this initiative was discussed, the conclusion was reached that what Milosevic offered did not guarantee equal rights for Bosnia and Herzegovina in this potential new rump Yugoslavia, or the equality of the peoples of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Page 17, line 12 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: The Bench would kindly ask the Defence to refrain from general political questions. As I mentioned before, the subject matter of our case is a different one, and we can't go in depth in these political questions, first of all, questions of political opportunities at that time. We have to restrict ourselves to facts at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] But Your Honour, in this case, the political background is crucial for the assigning of the guilt of the accused in this case. We have to show the attitude and the standpoint of other parties and who was actually pushing in which direction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: As I said, it's a question of facts, and we shouldn't discuss opinions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I will just have to quote the witness. So if the Prosecution considers that issue crucial and important, I think that we have the right to address the same issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed in the spirit the Bench just suggested to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Page 51, Monday's transcript, line 10, you state: "When Slovenia and Croatia began to secede from Yugoslavia, the attitude of the SDA was that should Croatia stay part of Yugoslavia, we shall continue to consider this state as Yugoslavia. Should Croatia secede, then the balance is destroyed and the state is no longer Yugoslavia, but rather Greater Serbia. Our view was that in this case, we could not remain in that state as part of Greater Serbia." I must ask you again, does this mean that the SDA associated the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina with the secession of Croatia, or made it dependent on the secession of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. As you have read out right now, the SDA thought, believed, that Bosnia-Herzegovina should not stay in Greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In your opinion, was it at that point that the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina became inevitable?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As Milosevic wasn't offering any other solutions, the initiative by Filipovic that I was talking about was a blueprint for this. So that seems to have remained the only possibility at that time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Does that mean that you proceeded with secession regardless of the will of one of the ethnic groups in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that is not correct. Please, if I may just finish, although the SDA, for example, had a large number of Bosniak votes, it did have a number of votes of other ethnic groups. The Serbian Democratic Party also contended that it had -- that most of its votes were Serbian, but that it had other votes, too, from other groups, which was clearly demonstrated by local elections in Prijedor. The same goes for the HDZ, or at least that's what they were claiming. This means that the Party for Democratic Action was not and could not be the only representative of the Bosnian people. So there is no equation sign between the SDA and Bosniaks. And there is no equation mark between the SDS and Serbs. So in the referendum, there were Serb members of parliament who also voted in favour, but the later results of the referendum showed that there were quite many Serbs also who voted in the referendum in favour of an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina. If we suppose that all Bosniaks and all Croats in Bosnia and Herzegovina gave their vote in favour, that would still be a lot less than 63 or 64 per cent, I can't remember now, which was the number of votes -- the percentage of the votes in favour. This implies that also, a significant part of Bosnian Serbs favoured an independent Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time of the referendum were representatives of the SDS absent from the parliament? We knew about the results of the plebiscite where 95 or 96 per cent of the Serbs voted for remaining in the common state, the shared state. So we're not speaking about here about the SDS but about the will of the Serbian people, and you were familiar with this at the time of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Counsel, with all due respect, I should like to remind you of the essential differences between the plebiscite of the Serbian people and the referendum which was held in Bosnia-Herzegovina. The plebiscite of the Serbian people was held, as far as I remember, as early as in November 1991, long time before any debate on the possible secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina was possible. The plebiscite was called by the Serb Democratic Party, which means that it was not called by any legal institution of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina at the time, but by a single political party. This plebiscite demonstrated clearly certain aspects of national segregation, because blue ballots were intended for Serbs, and yellow, I believe, for non-Serbs, which tells you how at the very stage of voting, there were already elements of segregation which obviously caused a certain amount of distrust amongst the non-Serb population. Moreover, if I remember, the result of the plebiscite was a hundred per cent. Allegedly, the turnout was a hundred per cent, and all of the voters voted in favour. And as far as I could observe by living in Prijedor, a significant number of Serbs didn't vote, did not turn out at the plebiscite. So the number -- the figure that you indicated, 95 or 96 per cent, could by no means be accurate.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: The information that you have, does it refer to the number of affirmative votes by the voters who turned out at the plebiscite, or to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the number of those who turned out compared to the overall size and number of the population?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In the interpretation of the election results of the Serbian Democratic Party, it was said that the overall Serb population voted in favour, voted affirmative at the plebiscite. We, on the other hand, did not have direct insight into the results of this election, because the Serb Democratic Party was the only body in charge of this election and processing its results. So on the basis of the interpretation given by them, it was possible to conclude that all Serb citizens turned out, and that all of them voted in favour.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You said that you did not have access to information. Did the SDS attempt to hide this information, or did they try to make it public?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that we did not have direct insight into the counting of the votes and the verification of the results, which the kind of work which is normally done by the relevant commissions at the level of municipalities and at the level of the republic. The Serbian Democratic Party did not have -- was not -- this plebiscite was not legitimate. The Serb Democratic Party attempted to make it legal and legitimate, but in actual fact, it was not. And this is what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What I'm trying to establish through this line of questioning is whether the SDA and HDZ, as representatives of the majority of the Croat and Bosniak population in Bosnia and Herzegovina knew at the time that one significant segment of the population was against the secession of Bosnia and Herzegovina from Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What we knew for sure was the fact that this was opposed by the Serbian Democratic Party, that is, its leadership. We're not even sure whether the overall membership of the Serbian Democratic Party was against this. We also knew that the Serbian Democratic Party was not the sole representative of the Serbian population. You cannot equate the SDS with the Serbian population.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: How about the HDZ and the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Likewise.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But they were also the only ones who decided on it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this decision was also made by all other party members who were represented at the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the statement by Mr. Alija Izetbegovic at the time who was the president of the Party of Democratic Action? I quote: "Bosnia is worth sacrificing peace in Bosnia."

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Give me just a moment to organise my response. If aggression should be underway against any country in Europe or somewhere else in the world, as was the case with Milosevic in Yugoslavia, and if anyone should attempt to obliterate a European country in this way, would it be possible for the president of the state in question to say that it is necessary to prepare ourselves to defend the country against its extinction? Because that is exactly what he meant when he said that.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So you are familiar with the statement that I just quoted given by Mr. Izetbegovic?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 69, line 19, Monday's transcript, you stated that the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina declared a state of immediate danger of war in April 1992. Is this correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I also stated, and if I didn't, let me do it now, that the exact date when the state of immediate danger of war was declared in Bosnia and Herzegovina was not known to me. So once again, I'm not sure whether it took place in April or sometime in mid-May that year.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. You said that you didn't have any military structure. Have you read the book written by Mr. Sefer Halilovic, "The Cunning Strategy"?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I have not.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Prijedor saw the formation of the Patriotic League as early as 1992?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What is the relationship between the Party of Democratic Action and the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Party of Democratic Action was one of the parties that supported the objectives and the aims of the Patriotic League; namely, the defence of the homeland.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is the SDA, at the same time, the founder of the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, the initiative came from Mr. Sefer Halilovic. And again, as far as I know, Mr. Sefer Halilovic was never a member of the Party for Democratic Action.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: On page 18, line 9, Monday's transcript, you make mention of an instruction issued by the presidency of Bosnia and Herzegovina that its citizens should not take part in the war against Croatia. Are you able to tell us when this instruction was issued? Approximately, at least.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that it could be the month of July, July 1991.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the number of mobilisations that were called up in 1991?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The number of mobilisations? In which area and at what time?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1991. I am referring to September, October, and November 1991.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am familiar with one such order, one callup, which was issued at the local level in the Prijedor municipality. That is one mobilisation that I'm familiar of. But I do not know anything about other mobilisations, that is, mobilisations in other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You told us something about who is in charge of calling up a mobilisation. Is it possible to call up a mobilisation at the local level? You also said that it was the municipal -- you said that the municipal secretariat for national defence was only an agency belonging to the ministry in question.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct, which means that a local secretariat could not, on its own, call up a mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What about the secretary of the secretariat for national defence? Was that Mr. Becir Medunjanin at the time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Becir Medunjanin was the secretary.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is Mr. Becir Medunjanin Bosniak by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: At the time, was Mr. Medunjanin a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he was. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Would it be an appropriate time for a break now.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] Yes, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Then the trial stands adjourned until 11.00 sharp.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please be seated. Before we restart, I have to announce a decision of the Chamber. The time limit for the cross-examination by the Defence expires tomorrow at 1:30. For obvious reasons, we have the witness only available for the two days, and so it's up to the Defence to decide which are the most important matters to raise. And additionally, we would ask -- you spoke about a board this morning, please present it to the Prosecution and the Bench before you present it to the witness. Thank you. We have new appearances on the side of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, for the record present in addition to myself and Ms. Karper is Pooja Bhalla, an intern with our office. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Dr. Mujadzic, can we continue now?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Are you familiar with the fact that in September 1991, the response to the mobilisation was over 80 per cent, and this response included Croats, a small number of Croats, but in terms of percentage, the same number of Bosniaks responded to the callup as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Does this relate to mobilisation in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Yes. The data I've just given refers to mobilisation in Prijedor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's the first time I see this information, but I find it to be very indicative. As I have said before, Bosniaks and Croats did respond to the mobilisation, and I provided the example of the gathering in Jaruge for the Territorial Defence under Colonel Colic but having noticed many of the mobilised wearing Chetnik insignia, and having heard their nationalistic and chauvinistic speeches made by some of the commanders and by Colonel Colic himself, the majority of those who responded to the callup, among the Bosniaks and Croats, as well as a certain number of Serbs, refused to go to the front line and refused to remain in the units when they heard about the aims of this mobilisation. Are you familiar with the makeup of the units?

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you. I cannot answer questions. I cannot testify from where I stand. Did a majority of the Serbs respond to the mobilisation? Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Even today, I have many Serbs among my friends and acquaintances. I know that a significant number of Serbs failed to respond to the mobilisation. They deserted and left Bosnia for third countries because they were in disagreement with the policies advocated by those who organised these mobilisations.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those Serbs who responded to the callup, were they given weapons on that occasion? Can you tell us anything about that?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, when I talked about mobilisation in Jaruge by Colonel Colic, not all of those who responded to the callup eventually joined the units. Many of them, when they heard about the aims of this mobilisation, and the aim was to go to the war in Croatia and fight against their neighbours and friends of yesterday, many gave up and did not join the units, which includes a number of Serbs, too.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Those who did join, were they given weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I assume they did, assuming that they joined the unit and they were going to the front line. Probably they were given weapons, but I did not witness this. I was not an eyewitness to this, so I cannot say for sure.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the people who joined the units, did they get any tanks, guns, Howitzers, rifles as part of the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The units at that time purported to be still the JNA, but their commanding staff and their tolerance for the presence of reservists of the JNA, people carrying insignia that were not JNA insignia, but rather Chetnik insignia, white eagles' insignia, extremist units led by Vojislav Seselj, all these people de facto turned the JNA into a Serbian ideological army under the ideology of Slobodan Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Maybe I was not clear enough. I have been trying to draw your attention to weapons and not to insignia statements or anything like that. What I want to ask you is did the JNA hide, conceal the fact, that it gave people rifles, guns, Howitzers, tanks, those people who did respond to the callup and who did join the units? Did the JNA do this secretly or publicly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whoever joined the units eventually, units of the Territorial Defence led by Colonel Colic, and I think the 43rd Brigade led by Colonel -- or at that time Second Lieutenant Arsic, of course, they were given weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did everyone who responded to the mobilisation and join the units, was everyone given weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I hope that I have already answered this question in my previous reply.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Why should the JNA, then, need to give weapons in secrecy to Serbs in the villages throughout the area as they did, as you have just described it?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we talking about assumptions or about facts? Our facts say that the JNA did, indeed, distribute weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So at the same time they distributed weapons to Serb, both secretly and publicly. Is that your testimony?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please do not try to interpret what I wanted to say. Please ask me directly about my interpretation. I never said this. It was you who said that the JNA armed members of the units that it had mobilised, as any other army would have done. And you said yourself that among the members of these units, there were not only Serbs. I know that there were Bosniaks and Croats who did go to the front line in Croatia. Therefore, the JNA distributed weapons to those people who responded to the mobilisation and accepted to go to the war in Croatia. And at that time, it was still legal. However, the JNA also illegally distributed weapons around Serbian villages and only to the Serbian population, which was not connected to what they were doing with those who responded to the mobilisation.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Did the majority of those who did respond to the mobilisation, were they Serbs?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I would like to continue now with a different issue, and I would like to ask you something related to what you stated on Monday, Monday's transcript page 21, line 25 through page 22, line 9. You contend that within the police forces and all other institutions, justice, financial institutions, social enterprises and institutions in Prijedor, as well as throughout Bosnia and Herzegovina, Bosniaks were unequally represented as compared to Serbs. Is it your testimony that in Bosnia and Herzegovina, the principle of equal representation was not applied or the rotation of personnel recruited from all the ethnic groups of Bosnia and Herzegovina, also known as the "national key"?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. In Bosnia, the national key did, indeed, exist, and this so-called national key implied that at the level of the republican organs of authority, if the president of the central committee of the communist party of Bosnia and Herzegovina, because we're talking about Tito's Yugoslavia, this implied that the president of the parliament was Serb, if the president of the central committee was a Bosniak and the president, prime minister, was a Croat. This was a parity that was upheld at the republican level, at least as far as the leading positions were concerned. However, speaking about percentage, the figures are related to the structure of the administration or the key positions within the administration. Therefore, it is not sufficient if the prime minister is Bosniak, as long as assistance to ministers, advisors, were in 80 or 90 out of a hundred cases Serbs or members of other ethnic groups. Because those bodies that create laws, make proposals for laws, constitute some sort of a fixed, permanent administration. Let's take the example of the U.S.A. It is the administration that remains a fixed point of reference and guarantees the stability of the state. If you change one man, you can't change the lot.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So even when Tito was still alive, the Bosniaks were neglected as concerns their appointments to leading positions?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was more evident at the local level than at the republican level. I will provide an example, an example of Prijedor, which is the situation I am most familiar with. Ever since the war, until 1990, so throughout 45 years, Bosniaks were appointed to the position of the chief of police only twice, which means that a Serb was appointed to the same position 43 times. In all the key structures, important positions, within the local police, out of a total of a hundred employees, in about 10 or 12 important positions, there were only 2 Bosniaks, and the remaining 8 positions were always, even at such times when certain positions were traditionally held by members of Serb ethnicity. Let's take the example of municipal administration. Over a total of 336 employees of Prijedor municipality, only about 70-something were Bosniaks, part of which were alleged Yugoslavs. And there were between 15 and 20 representatives of Croat ethnicity. But there were over 200 Serbs. So even this administration reflects what I have said before. And just another final example: I could name a lot of such examples. Since 1945, so we're talking about Tito's Yugoslavia, in Prijedor municipality, the position of the president of the municipality, Cehajic, as far as I can remember, was only the third or fourth Bosniak person in that position, and the remaining 40 times the president was appointed, it was always Serbs who were appointed. I think once it may have been a Croat. So this is a very typical occurrence. At these levels, it was reflected in most of the structures in most municipalities in Bosnia-Herzegovina. However, it wasn't this that the Bosniaks really minded. Even this kind of Yugoslavia was accepted by the Bosniaks. The problem was that what Milosevic actually offered was a lot less than what I have now been speaking about.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Is this insufficient representation of Bosniaks in administration positions, was it conditioned by the fact that Bosniaks were mostly into private enterprises; and thus, they controlled most of the money in circulation in Prijedor municipality?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you've said is correct, but that is a result and not a cause. The fact that Bosniaks, the reason that Bosniaks couldn't find employment in the structure of the state was mostly because they were into private business. But they should have been in a position to influence the taxes raised from private business, as is normal, common practice throughout the world.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: I think we can agree that in the former system, no entrepreneur could affect the level of taxes, regardless of his nationality.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I said referred to the new system, a system that was supposed to be a democratic one, and certain changes were supposed to take place. I wasn't talking about the previous system. As far as the previous system is concerned, I agree that no one could effect this, apart from the administration. And I have already said who held the most important positions on this administration.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let us return to the issue of weapons and armament. We have reached the conclusion that all those who responded to the mobilisation and joined the units were given weapons, that all Bosniaks and -- had all Bosniaks and all Croats decided to respond to the mobilisation, would all of them have been given weapons?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, probably they would have all been given weapons.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Can we, in that case, blame the JNA for not arming Muslims and Croats?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOUMJIAN
utterances.text: Objection. Argumentative.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I withdraw.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Sustained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You say that the Territorial Defence was -- constituted the army of the republic. What about the armed forces of the Socialist Federative Republic of Yugoslavia? Did they not belong to one and the same system, to a unique system of the military, and is it not true that the Territorial Defence units were part of, and subordinate to, the JNA units in case of imminent threat of war?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I use the expression "the army of the republic," I was being metaphorical. The fact remains that the Territorial Defence was organised according to the republican principle. It was organised on the basis of the republics. And the JNA had its units deployed in various barracks throughout Yugoslavia, whereas the Territorial Defence was organised in the republics, the Slovenians, for instance, had the Territorial Defence of Slovenia, and so on and so forth. And what you say -- on the other hand, what you say is true in cases of war or imminent threat of war, the assumption was that the Territorial Defence would be made part of a unified system of command. They would not be -- be opposed to each other. This organisation of the Territorial Defence reflected the idea of Tito, according to which each citizen of the country was the subject, so to speak, of the national defence. So the Territorial Defence units were related and connected to the territory where they were actually organised. But, the assumption was not, of course, that the Territorial Defence unit in a given area, as was the Territorial Defence unit of Colonel Colic, should go to war in Croatia, for example, which happened. So this principle of national defence, which was established during Tito's Yugoslavia, was impaired in the example that I just gave you. But there were cases of similar activity on the part of the JNA even before these events.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: We established, to go back to the SDA, that you were elected the first president of the SDA after the elections, and that Mr. Kapetanovic, Nijaz and Mr. Mevludin Sejmenovic were elected your deputies. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was another round of elections the next year in August of 1991. And once again, you were elected president of the party. Your deputies or the vice-presidents were Muharem Keric, Brafo Dzafic [phoen], and Mr. Hasan Talundzic. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Would you be so kind and correct me.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Kapetanovic and Sejmenovic were once again elected vice-presidents of the party.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But was there a change in this structure at one point in time; and if so, when?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, there was no such change at any point in time.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: So Mr. Kapetanovic remained as your vice-president throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: What was the position of Mr. Talundzic in the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, and to the best of my knowledge, he was an ordinary member of the party with no specific function.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a deputy to the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were a deputy to the Chamber of Citizens in this assembly?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: There was also a Chamber of Municipalities as part of this assembly, the assembly of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: When you were present at the sessions of this assembly, was there any discussion about a possible introduction of one more chamber, the Chamber of Peoples, whose objective would be to guarantee the constitutional equality of the constituent peoples of Bosnia-Herzegovina? Was this issue ever debated at any of the sessions which you attended?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think I need a few moments to recall, to remember, this issue in order to be able to respond to this question. I'm afraid I cannot answer with certainty, but I believe that the issue was debated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was there ever any talk about the possible establishment of the council for national equality whose work was envisaged pursuant to the already-made amendments to the constitution, if you can recall?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, I cannot speak with certainty, but it seems to me that that issue was also debated.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Do you know that, at the first session of the anti-fascist council of the national liberation force in Yugoslavia who established in Mrkonjic Grad in 1943 that Yugoslavia was not only a Croat -- that Bosnia and Herzegovina was not only a Bosnian, a Croat, or a Serb country, but it was Bosnian, Croat, and Serbian at the same time, and that as such, it would be made part of Yugoslavia? This was the legal constitutional basis of all of the constitutions of Bosnia and Herzegovina which were subsequently adopted, and this principle was respected and applied even in 1990 and 1991, that it was still in force. Are you familiar with this fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me go back to the issue of referendum, please. According to you, who are aware of this principle, the decision to have a referendum against the will of one of the peoples represented in the assembly, did it not constitute the contravention of this constitutional principle? You have mentioned the fact that there were individual Serbs, members of other parties, who were opposed to this. But if you intend to include this in your answer, will you please tell us the figures? How many of such Serbs there were members of other parties, and how many of that did, in fact, participate in the voting of the decision whereby it was decided that the referendum would be called?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Now we are entering the area of the legality of the decision to have a referendum, which is a rather complex legal issue. In order for me to be able to fully and adequately respond to your question, we would first have to define the concept of representatives of the Serbian people. Do you consider the Serbian Democratic Party to be the representative of the Serbian people? Because apart from the Serbian Democratic Party, then and now, there is a number of parties which in their name contain the word "Serb" but there were other parties that were not described as "Serb" parties who did not have any national or ethnic description in their title. So we are faced with the problem of defining the concept of the representatives of the Serbian people.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try to clarify. I am referring to the representatives of the Serbian people who advocated the attitude of the Serbian population expressed at the plebiscite.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, first of all, I think that we concluded that the plebiscite was not legal, that it was not based in law. Thereby, we have to question its legitimacy. I think we have already established that a large segment of the population, the Serbian population, did not turn out, which renders its results debatable. This plebiscite was conducted by a single political party. Furthermore, I do not remember that this referendum had, at any point in time, had its representatives, elected representatives. So I think that your question is misconstrued to begin with.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Let me try with another question. Are you familiar that a two-third majority is required for the passing of any constitutional amendments in Bosnia and Herzegovina? So in cases of such referendum, at least 60 per cent of the electorate should vote in favour of the constitutional amendment proposed. However, the overall turnout for the referendum for the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina was over 64 per cent, so it was less than the number which was required for the affirmative vote.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, the decision to go to a referendum did not require a two-thirds majority. The decision did not concern any constitutional amendment. It was merely a decision to have a referendum, whereby the population was given an opportunity to express its opinion on an issue which was debated at the referendum. So the subject of the referendum did not concern any constitutional changes.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: However, the results of the referendum should have -- were supposed to lead eventually to constitutional amendments?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's another issue.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You touched upon the issue of legitimacy of the referendum. Did this referendum legitimise any constitutional changes by its results? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not competent to discuss the issue of legitimacy of the referendum. The legality and the legitimacy of the referendum, the decision thereon, and its results were discussed by an independent commission, the Badinter [realtime transcript read in error "a"] Commission, if you remember. If my memory serves me right, the commission was established by the European Community. This commission approved the results of the referendum; and likewise, approved both the legitimacy and the legality of the referendum.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Was the decision of this commission a political one or a legal one? Did it take into account the valid constitution of Bosnia and Herzegovina at the time, if you know?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SCHOMBURG
utterances.text: Please, refer to facts only and not to the opinion of the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [In English] I withdraw the question, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, looking at the English transcript, the interpreter probably did not hear the name Badinter, the Badinter Commission. I can only see the word "commission" in the word. The name should be added. It's Badinter.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: You were the president of the municipal board of the SDA in Prijedor. You were a deputy to the Chamber of Citizens in the parliament of Bosnia and Herzegovina. You were also a member of the main board of the SDA, president of the regional committee for the Bosnian Krajina on behalf of the SDA. Is this correct? Are these the positions that you have held, with respect to the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two of the positions that you indicated are related to the SDA. The fourth one is my function as a deputy, which is a state function, a state position.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: As far as state functions are concerned, were you also president of the municipal commission for appointments to the Municipal Assembly in Prijedor?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I was not. It was not possible for me to have that function, because I was not a deputy to the municipal parliament. As a republican deputy, I could only attend such sessions as a visitor. I could not play any part in the decision-making process, nor could I make any proposals to that effect.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: Thank you for this correction. My information may not be right. Are you familiar with the procedure of appointing persons to various municipal functions? Which appointments were subjects of the negotiations in which you participated as a member of the SDA?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The appointment procedure as regards municipal positions is a very complicated one. Let me just emphasise that I only partly participated in such negotiations. At the beginning, it was a commission whose member I was, but this commission was followed by a number of other commissions whose member I was not. Speaking of the negotiations. As for the appointments themselves, the initiative comes from the municipal board of a party, which initiative is then examined by the municipal board of deputies who then decide whether they would support or oppose this decision at the local parliament. And the meetings of these deputies were attended by several people, and then -- and they decided to which candidate they would give their support. The voting was always secret. And out of several nominations, this club, this board of deputies selected the candidate that they intended to support at the session of the parliament.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
utterances.text: But it is true, is it not, that the party also nominated the officials whose appointments were not voted at the session of the Municipal Assembly? I am referring to the position of the chief of the public security station, for instance. His appointment could not be discussed at the Municipal Assembly. What was the procedure in this case?

utterances.speaker: MIRSAD MUJADZIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know -- I'm sorry, I believe that I have explained this procedure of appointments in my previous testimony. If necessary, I'll be happy to repeat it.

utterances.speaker: UNKNOWN EXAMINER
